question: What is the main problem that happens in all types of shock?

options.A: Not enough oxygen getting to body cells
options.B: Too much carbon dioxide stored in the lungs

explanation: Shock happens when the body fails to deliver enough oxygen to meet the basic needs of its tissues. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h1)

question: Why does metabolic acidosis happen when cells lack oxygen for a long time?

options.B: Cells without oxygen produce extra lactic acid
options.C: The lungs hold onto too much nitrogen
options.D: The kidneys stop filtering normal proteins

explanation: When cells lack oxygen, they switch to an energy pathway that produces lactic acid as a byproduct, which lowers blood pH. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h1)

question: During which stage of shock does the body successfully keep blood flowing to vital organs?
explanation: In the compensated stage, the body's natural reflexes keep blood pressure and flow normal for critical organs despite the underlying problem. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h2)

question: What happens in the body when shock moves into the progressive stage?

options.A: The body's defenses fail and organs do not get enough blood
options.B: Blood pressure suddenly returns to normal on its own
options.C: Cellular metabolism goes back to normal instantly
options.D: Kidneys produce a lot of dilute urine

explanation: As the body's energy reserves run out, it can no longer keep blood flowing properly to all tissues, leading to dropping blood pressure and failing organs. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h2)

question: Which type of shock involves severe widening of blood vessels and a shortage of active blood volume?
explanation: Distributive shock occurs when blood vessels relax and open up too much, making the blood space bigger than the available fluid volume. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h3)

question: A patient has a large blood clot blocking blood flow from the right side of the heart. What type of shock is this?
explanation: A pulmonary embolism creates a physical block that stops normal blood flow through the heart and lungs, which defines obstructive shock. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h3)

question: What is an early sign that a patient going into shock is not getting enough blood flow to their tissues?
explanation: The heart beats faster early on as the nervous system tries to make up for dropping blood volume or pressure. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h4)

question: Why do patients often pass very little urine in the early stages of fluid-loss shock?

options.A: The kidneys hold onto fluid to keep blood flowing to the brain and heart
options.B: Kidney filtration speeds up and dries out the bladder
options.C: Urine production stops because the tubes spasm
options.D: Bladder muscles relax and hold urine inside

explanation: Stress hormones direct blood away from the kidneys to protect vital organs like the brain and heart, which naturally lowers urine output. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h4)

question: What is the first nursing priority when caring for a patient who is starting to go into shock?

options.A: Give prescribed oral antibiotics right away
options.B: Make sure the airway is clear and give high-flow oxygen
options.C: Lay the patient flat on their stomach
options.D: Get the patient ready for discharge

explanation: Airway, breathing, and circulation are always the primary steps in any emergency to make sure oxygen reaches starved tissues. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h5)

question: Why is putting in a urinary catheter important when managing a patient in shock?

options.A: It brings blood pressure back up inside the kidneys
options.B: It stops urinary tract infections completely
options.C: It lets nurses measure how well the kidneys are getting blood hour by hour
options.D: It removes the need to give IV fluids

explanation: Urine output gives a direct, real-time look at how well blood is flowing to vital internal organs, especially the kidneys. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h5)

question: What is the main goal of giving vasopressor drugs to a patient in shock?

options.D: To help the kidneys pass water quickly

explanation: Vasopressors narrow blood vessels, which raises resistance in the circulatory system and helps push up dangerously low blood pressure. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h6)

question: When is an inotropic drug like dobutamine most useful for a patient in shock?

options.A: To kill bacteria in blood infections
options.B: To help the heart muscle pump harder when it is failing
options.C: To stop severe bleeding from a torn artery

explanation: Inotropes make the heart muscle squeeze with more force, which increases the amount of blood pumped out when the heart is weak. [learn more](GNS112_U7_T3#GNS112_U7_T3_h6)
